questions.title: What is the 'legislature knows how' canon of statutory interpretation and how is it applied?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, the court concludes that only the Commissioner—not the employee—can seek "average daily wage penalties" under Minnesota's Payment of Wages Act (§ 181.101). Part of the court's reasoning relies on the fact that other Minnesota statutes (§§ 181.13 and 181.14) explicitly authorize employees to seek penalties, so the legislature's failure to include similar language in § 181.101 must be intentional. The court cites this as the "legislature knows how" canon, referencing Lagasse v. Horton. I understand the basic idea that expressio unius est exclusio alterius, but I'm confused about how this canon works in practice. Is this a standalone canon or just an application of negative implication? And how do courts decide when it's appropriate to infer legislative intent from the presence of language in one statute but absence in another, versus assuming the legislature just made a drafting oversight?

questions.title: Can a federal appeals court raise Article III jurisdictional concerns like mootness sua sponte when neither party has briefed the issue?
questions.question_body: In this case, the Eighth Circuit vacated the district court's grant of summary judgment on Cohen's MFLSA claim and remanded for the district court to determine its own jurisdiction, specifically whether Cohen's claim for statutory penalties is moot. The court says it has a "serious concern regarding our jurisdiction" even though Cohen was apparently still actively pursuing this claim and neither party raised the issue. I always thought courts generally decide the issues parties present to them. Under what authority can a federal court raise jurisdictional concerns on its own? Is there a distinction between standing and mootness in terms of when courts must raise them sua sponte versus when they can choose to? And does the fact that penalties under the MFLSA are payable to the Commissioner rather than to Cohen affect the analysis?

questions.title: Does a plaintiff have Article III standing to seek civil penalties that are payable to the government rather than to the plaintiff?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the standing analysis in this case. Cohen is seeking statutory penalties under the MFLSA, but the parties agree these penalties would be payable to the Commissioner, not to Cohen personally. The court cites Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw for the proposition that civil penalties paid to the government can still provide redress to citizen plaintiffs because they deter future violations. But Judge Kobes's concurrence expresses skepticism about whether Laidlaw really applies given differences between the penalties at issue there and those under the MFLSA. How does the redressability prong of standing work when the plaintiff doesn't personally receive any money? Is the deterrence of future violations really sufficient injury to satisfy Article III, or does this depend on the specific statutory context?

questions.title: How does the voluntary cessation doctrine apply when an employer pays owed wages but the challenged policy may still be in effect?
questions.question_body: The court discusses whether Consilio's payment of Cohen's overtime wages and liquidated damages moots his claim for civil penalties. The court notes that voluntary cessation of a challenged practice doesn't automatically deprive a federal court of jurisdiction, citing City of Mesquite v. Aladdin's Castle. But the court also says the claim "might become moot" if it's "absolutely clear" the wrongful conduct won't recur. The opinion then remands because there's a dispute about whether Consilio's violative overtime policy is still in place. I'm confused about how the burden works here. Does the defendant bear the burden of showing it's "absolutely clear" the conduct won't recur? And what would Consilio need to show to meet that standard—just that they paid Cohen, or that they actually changed their company-wide policy? Also, how does this interact with the fact that the penalty claim is about deterrence rather than compensation?

questions.title: What is the consequence of failing to provide legal authority or argument for a claim on appeal?
questions.question_body: The court quickly dismisses Cohen's MWTA claim by stating he "points to no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties under this statute" and provides "no meaningful argument in support of reversal," citing Milligan v. City of Red Oak for the proposition that unsupported assertions are waived. But Cohen did raise this claim below and the district court addressed it. I'm confused about the standard for waiver on appeal. Is this issue preservation, appellate waiver, or something else? How much argument and authority does a party need to provide to avoid waiver? Does it matter that the district court ruled on the claim? And is there any difference between failing to cite legal authority and failing to make any argument at all?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff seek different injunctive relief in a summary judgment brief than what was requested in the complaint?
questions.question_body: Cohen originally sought certain specific forms of injunctive relief in his complaint, but then requested different relief—withdrawing the 2019 policy—in his summary judgment briefing. The court says this issue is not properly before it, citing InfoDeli, LLC for the proposition that "new claims are properly raised through amended complaints, not opposition briefs" and referencing Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a). I'm confused about the line between modifying a claim and raising an entirely new one. Why is requesting different injunctive relief treated as a "new claim" rather than just a refinement of the existing claim? Would this have been permissible if Cohen had sought leave to amend under Rule 15(a)? And what should a plaintiff do when they realize during litigation that the relief they originally requested isn't quite what they need?
